summary: Defines the Content-Duration MIME header, which states how long a piece of timed media such as audio or video plays. It lets a receiver know the length without opening the content. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 3803.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2424 defines a MIME header that gives the duration of timed media such as audio or video in seconds. A recipient can read the value without opening the media, but the sender-provided duration is not guaranteed to be exact; RFC 3803 later obsoleted this memo.

how long is a voice message

subtitle: A MIME field that states the playback duration of timed media.

tldr.problem: A recipient may want to know the duration of audio or video without opening the media content.
tldr.mechanism: The Content-Duration MIME header carries a sender-determined duration in seconds, with no unit marker.

sections.title: A Duration Value in the MIME Header
sections.content:
Audio and video have a time duration. Although some encodings include duration information or allow it to be calculated from the data, a MIME header can make a sender-determined duration available without processing the content.

The field is intended for timed media, typically audio or video, and its value gives the duration in seconds without a units indication.
sections.plainLanguage: The header puts a media duration in the message so a recipient can see it without opening the content. The number is in seconds.

sections.title: Syntax and Meaning
sections.content:
The syntax is Content-Duration: followed by one to ten decimal digits. For example, Content-Duration: 33 represents 33 seconds. The theoretical upper bound stated by the RFC is 2147483647.

The value should be exact, but an exact duration cannot be known without opening and playing the content. The receiver's use of the field is a local implementation matter.
sections.plainLanguage: A value such as Content-Duration: 33 means the sender reports 33 seconds. To know the exact duration, a recipient has to inspect and play the content.

sections.title: Use with Voice Messages
sections.content: The RFC identifies the audio/32KADPCM subtype used by VPIM as a useful case for Content-Duration. Making the duration available in the header can help a recipient view the length of a voice message without opening its audio content, including with a simple MIME or non-MIME desktop.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail program can show the reported length of a voice message before the recipient opens the audio.

sections.title: Trust and Privacy
sections.content: The duration is supplied by the sender, and the RFC says it cannot be trusted to determine the exact size of the media data. The data itself must be examined to determine its exact length. In some environments, including the duration in a header may create a security issue, so the sender may choose not to include it.
sections.plainLanguage: The value is not verified, so do not use it to determine the actual data size. In some cases, revealing a duration in a header may also be a security concern.
